questions.prompt: Marie Antoinette really said "Let them eat cake".
questions.explain: There is no evidence she said it; a similar line appears in Rousseau's Confessions, written when she was a child.

questions.prompt: Mahatma Gandhi wrote "Be the change you wish to see in the world".
questions.explain: The line is a modern paraphrase; nothing like it appears in his writings in those words.

questions.prompt: Albert Einstein defined insanity as doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results.
questions.explain: The saying is not found in Einstein's writings; it appears in recovery literature from the 1980s.

questions.prompt: Voltaire wrote "I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it".
questions.explain: It was written by his biographer Evelyn Beatrice Hall in 1906 to sum up his attitude.

questions.prompt: Sherlock Holmes says "Elementary, my dear Watson" in Arthur Conan Doyle's stories.
questions.explain: The exact phrase never appears in the original stories; it was popularised by later films.

questions.prompt: In Casablanca, Humphrey Bogart says "Play it again, Sam".
questions.explain: The actual lines are closer to "Play it, Sam" and "You played it for her, you can play it for me".

questions.prompt: In The Empire Strikes Back, Darth Vader says "Luke, I am your father".
questions.explain: The line in the film is "No, I am your father."

questions.prompt: Captain Kirk says "Beam me up, Scotty" in the original Star Trek series.
questions.explain: That exact phrase was never said in the series, although similar orders were.

questions.prompt: Apollo 13's crew radioed "Houston, we have a problem".
questions.explain: The real words were "Houston, we've had a problem"; the present-tense version comes from the 1995 film.

questions.prompt: Charles Darwin coined the phrase "survival of the fittest".
questions.explain: Herbert Spencer coined it in 1864; Darwin adopted it in later editions of On the Origin of Species.

questions.prompt: Winston Churchill said "Success is not final, failure is not fatal: it is the courage to continue that counts".
questions.explain: The International Churchill Society finds no evidence he said it.

questions.prompt: Aristotle wrote "We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit".
questions.explain: The words are historian Will Durant's 1926 summary of Aristotle's ideas.

questions.prompt: Leonardo da Vinci said "Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication".
questions.explain: There is no source linking the saying to Leonardo; it surfaced centuries later.

questions.prompt: Walt Disney said "If you can dream it, you can do it".
questions.explain: The line was written by Disney Imagineer Tom Fitzgerald for an Epcot attraction in 1983.

questions.prompt: Henry Ford said "If I had asked people what they wanted, they would have said faster horses".
questions.explain: No record of Ford saying it has been found; it appears only decades after his death.

questions.prompt: Bill Gates said "640K ought to be enough for anybody".
questions.explain: Gates has denied ever saying it, and no source has been found.

questions.prompt: As a boy, George Washington confessed "I cannot tell a lie" about chopping down a cherry tree.
questions.explain: The story was invented by his biographer Mason Locke Weems, published after Washington's death.

questions.prompt: King Louis XIV declared "L'État, c'est moi" ("I am the state").
questions.explain: Historians regard it as apocryphal; there is no reliable record of him saying it.

questions.prompt: Galileo muttered "And yet it moves" after recanting before the Inquisition.
questions.explain: The story first appears more than a century after his death.

questions.prompt: Albert Einstein said "Two things are infinite: the universe and human stupidity".
questions.explain: The quote is unsourced and does not appear in Einstein's writings.

questions.prompt: Edmund Burke wrote "The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing".
questions.explain: It is not in Burke's writings; the earliest versions date from the 20th century.

questions.prompt: "Et tu, Brute?" is a line written by William Shakespeare.
questions.explain: Caesar says it in Shakespeare's play Julius Caesar; there is no evidence the real Caesar said it.

questions.prompt: Neil Armstrong was the first person to speak words from the surface of the Moon.
questions.explain: His famous line came as he stepped onto the surface in July 1969.

questions.prompt: "The pen is mightier than the sword" was first written by William Shakespeare.
questions.explain: The phrase comes from Edward Bulwer-Lytton's play Richelieu (1839).

questions.prompt: "I think, therefore I am" was written by René Descartes.
questions.explain: It appears in his Discourse on the Method (1637), first in French.

questions.prompt: Mark Twain wrote "The coldest winter I ever spent was a summer in San Francisco".
questions.explain: No evidence links it to Twain; it began circulating long after his death.

questions.prompt: Queen Victoria is reliably recorded saying "We are not amused".
questions.explain: The only source is a much later diary account; her biographers doubt she said it.

questions.prompt: "Elementary" appears in the Sherlock Holmes stories, even though "Elementary, my dear Watson" does not.
questions.explain: Holmes says "Elementary" in The Crooked Man (1893), but never with "my dear Watson" attached.
